title: Quant Dev vs Researcher vs Trader vs FPGA
tagline: The four main hiring tracks at HFT firms — what each does day-to-day and what they're tested on.

concept.analogy: A Formula 1 team is the cleanest analogy. The driver (trader) makes real-time decisions and owns the result on track. The race engineers and aerodynamicists (researchers) design the car and strategy from data. The mechanics and software/hardware engineers (quant devs / systems / FPGA) build the car and the pit systems and make them blisteringly fast and reliable. You can be world-class at any of these roles — and they all need each other to win.
paragraphs: HFT firms hire across several tracks. The lines blur between firms, but the archetypes are: Quantitative Trader, Quantitative Researcher, Quantitative Developer / Software Engineer, and specialist Systems / FPGA / Hardware engineers. Knowing which one you're aiming at tells you exactly what to study — because the interviews differ sharply.

Quantitative Trader: owns strategy decisions, risk, and P&L in real time. Hired heavily on probability, mental math, and market-making games rather than deep coding. Often hired straight from undergrad at firms like Optiver, IMC, SIG, Jane Street.

Quantitative Researcher: builds the models and signals from data — alpha research, backtesting, calibration. Heavy on statistics, probability, and (depending on the firm) ML and stochastic processes, plus strong Python. Tested on math/stats depth and research judgment.

Quantitative Developer / Low-Latency SWE: builds and optimizes the trading system — feed handlers, order books, the hot path. This is the most C++-and-systems-heavy track: memory model, lock-free, cache behavior, and systems design. Firms like HRT, Citadel Securities, Jump, Radix weight this most.

Systems / FPGA / Hardware: the deepest specialists — kernel-bypass networking, FPGA/ASIC, deterministic latency. Tested on Verilog/VHDL, digital design, and networking. A smaller, very specialized track.
points: Trader → probability, mental math, market-making games; fast decisions under uncertainty.
Researcher → statistics, probability, signal/ML research, Python; rigor and research taste.
Quant Dev / SWE → modern C++, low-latency systems, the memory model, systems design.
Systems / FPGA → networking, hardware, deterministic latency, Verilog/VHDL.
concept.keyIdea: Pick a primary track early. The probability + microstructure core is shared, but Dev/Systems roles demand low-latency C++ and systems mastery, while Trader/Researcher roles demand probability, mental math, and statistics.

deepDive.intro: This module is built so you can follow any track. Here's how the sections map, and how the tracks overlap.

steps.title: The shared core (everyone)
steps.detail: Market microstructure (order books, matching, market data) and probability/EV are assumed knowledge for every role. Sections 'Foundations', 'Market Microstructure', and 'Probability, Stats & Mental Math' are for everyone.

steps.title: If you're aiming Quant Dev / Low-Latency SWE
steps.detail: Live in 'Modern C++ for Low Latency', 'Low-Latency Systems Engineering', and 'Trading System Architecture'. You must be able to write correct lock-free code, reason about cache and the memory model, and design a tick-to-trade pipeline live. Microstructure and basic probability are still expected.

steps.title: If you're aiming Quant Researcher
steps.detail: Go deep in 'Probability, Stats & Mental Math' and 'Strategies & Quant Research' (signals, stat-arb, backtesting). Strong Python and statistics matter more than C++. You should still understand microstructure intimately because your signals live in it.

steps.title: If you're aiming Quant Trader
steps.detail: Master probability, mental math, and market-making games (the games lesson is for you), plus microstructure. Coding is lighter but you should be comfortable with logic and quick estimation. Calibration and disciplined risk-taking are the graded skills.

steps.title: If you're aiming Systems / FPGA
steps.detail: Everything in 'Low-Latency Systems Engineering' plus the networking and hardware lessons, and the FPGA lesson specifically. You'll go beyond this module into digital design, but the systems mindset here is the foundation.

notes.title: You don't have to choose forever
notes.detail: Many people move between tracks (dev→trader, researcher→dev). But for a specific interview loop, prepare for that loop's emphasis. A researcher loop won't grill you on lock-free queues; a dev loop won't grill you on stochastic calculus.

pitfalls: Preparing 'a bit of everything' shallowly. Depth in your target track's core beats breadth.
Devs neglecting probability/microstructure — you'll still be asked, and it signals you understand the product.
Traders/researchers thinking they need zero coding — comfort with Python (research) or clean logic (trading) is expected.

interviewQuestions.q: An interviewer asks: 'Why the developer track and not trading or research?' How do you give a strong answer?
a: Anchor it in genuine interest and evidence, not flattery. Strong answers connect what energizes you to what the role actually is: e.g., 'I love making systems fast and correct — I've spent time profiling C++, writing lock-free structures, and chasing tail latency, and the idea that a microsecond is worth real money is motivating. I find building the engine more compelling than making the discretionary calls.'

Back it with a concrete artifact (a project: a matching engine, a low-latency parser, a benchmark you optimized). Show you understand the trade-off you're choosing — you're opting into deep systems work over direct P&L ownership — and that it's a deliberate, informed choice.
followups: What project best demonstrates your low-latency skills?
Where do you see the dev/researcher boundary at this firm?

interviewQuestions.q: How much do the researcher and developer roles overlap at an HFT firm, and where do they hand off?
a: They overlap heavily around the strategy: researchers design signals and models and validate them in backtests; developers turn those into production code that runs on the hot path within a latency budget, and build the data/backtesting infrastructure researchers rely on.

The hand-off is usually: researcher specifies and prototypes (often Python) → developer productionizes and optimizes (C++), ensuring the live system reproduces backtest behavior. At smaller firms one person may do both ('quant dev'); at larger firms they're distinct but tightly collaborating roles. Good devs understand the research; good researchers understand the latency/feasibility constraints.

interviewQuestions.q: What's the day-to-day difference between a quant developer and a quant researcher at an HFT firm?
a: A quant developer builds and operates the trading system: the feed handlers, order books, strategy engine, OMS, and the low-latency C++/systems infrastructure that runs the firm's strategies in production with correctness and minimal latency/jitter. Their day is dominated by software engineering, performance work, debugging production issues, and reliability — they make the machine fast and correct.

A quant researcher discovers and validates the *strategies and signals*: they analyze data, build and backtest models, find alpha, calibrate parameters, and study execution and risk — largely offline/research work in Python/C++ with strong statistics. The two collaborate tightly: research produces the signal/parameters; development turns them into a fast, safe, production strategy. Some firms blur the line (researcher-developers), and traders sit alongside making/monitoring real-time decisions. Knowing which role you want determines whether you weight prep toward C++/systems or probability/stats/modeling.

problems.title: Match the skill profile to the role
problems.statement: For each candidate, recommend the best-fit HFT track (quant dev, quant researcher, quant trader, or low-latency/FPGA engineer) and the single most important skill to deepen: (a) loves C++, memory models, and squeezing nanoseconds; (b) strong in statistics/ML, enjoys data and modeling, codes in Python; (c) thrives on fast decisions under uncertainty, great at mental math and games; (d) fascinated by digital logic, Verilog, and wire-speed processing.
problems.hint: Map each profile to the role whose core bar it already matches, then name the highest-leverage gap to close.

approach: (a) Quant developer / low-latency systems — deepen the C++ cost/memory model and systems performance (caches, lock-free, measurement). (b) Quant researcher — deepen rigorous backtesting/statistics and avoiding lookahead/overfitting, plus enough engineering to productionize. (c) Quant trader — deepen probability/EV, fast mental math, and market-making game intuition, and practice them out loud under time pressure. (d) FPGA/hardware engineer — deepen RTL (Verilog/VHDL), timing closure, and the FPGA/CPU boundary plus the microstructure the logic implements.

The meta-point: each profile already matches a track's core bar, so the highest-leverage move is to *go deep* on that track's signature skill rather than spreading thin. Adjacent literacy still helps (a trader who can code a clean function, a dev who understands basic probability), but you win by being clearly excellent at your track's bar.

problems.title: Trace a signal from research to production
problems.statement: A researcher finds that order-flow imbalance predicts the next 200ms price move with a small but real edge. Describe the hand-off and the responsibilities of the researcher, the quant developer, the trader, and (optionally) an FPGA engineer to get this live safely — and where it could go wrong if the roles don't coordinate.
problems.hint: Research validates the signal/params; dev productionizes it fast and correct; risk/trader gate and monitor it live; FPGA may host the hottest part.

approach: Researcher: validates the imbalance signal with an honest backtest (realistic fills, costs, no lookahead), quantifies its edge/decay, and produces a compact parameter set (thresholds, sizing, horizon). Quant developer: implements the signal on the hot path as a fast, branch-predictable computation over those parameters, wires it into the strategy engine/OMS, ensures it's allocation-free and deterministic, and makes the same code run in backtest and live. Trader/risk: sets position and loss limits, monitors live P&L and behavior versus backtest, and can flatten/halt via the kill switch. FPGA engineer (optional): if latency-critical, implements the parse + imbalance trigger + risk gate in hardware for tens-of-ns response, with the CPU arming parameters.

Failure modes from poor coordination: the live implementation differs from the backtested logic (so tested edge ≠ live behavior); the signal decays faster than the system can act (latency mismatch); parameters aren't safely swappable; risk limits don't reflect the strategy's true exposure; or no one monitors live-vs-backtest divergence, so silent decay or a bug erodes capital. Tight role coordination — research correctness, dev fidelity/speed, trader/risk oversight — is what turns a backtested edge into safe live P&L.
